doc.title: Greg Caputo interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 14, 1998

title: Teaching discipline and adapting to each student
summary: He explains discipline in structured jazz, how he teaches each student differently, and which students became working players.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Discipline in jazz playing. That’s an interesting concept. How do you pass that idea on to students, that there has to be discipline in a music that supposedly is all about freedom?

Well it’s a structured music. It’s not totally free. I mean I just can’t go in and play anything I want, I listen to the other people, and I have to have discipline to be able to respond, call and respond, and feel. It’s discipline, make no mistake about it, that all of the great jazz masters have discipline in their playing. To convey that to students, to communicate that, it’s not easy. Usually they have to get their feet wet and they’ll come back to me and say I’m in trouble. I need this discipline. And then I can start a foundation and give them the rudiments and the discipline of reading, and how that gives them self control in their playing.

Is it hard to convey to a young up and coming student who’s really feeling that I’ve got this stuff down, not only the discipline but also the realities that some day they may be required to do this kind of playing, and you better be able to do it? Do they tend to not believe you until they get out and see that?

Every student is different first of all, I don’t have one method. I sit down and I talk with a student before I accept them, and it gives me some idea of the direction I have to take © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

with them. I have many older students that come to me, and they come to me with situations they’ve been in, it might be a technique that they need to polish, it might be reading, or it might be just how to handle themselves with other musicians. And I cover all that. Some of the younger students, right now they’re involved in a school show. They might come to me with just a piece of music they want me to play for them, which I won’t do, I’ll give them key parts of it, and eventually I’ll let them play but I won’t play it for them. I adjust my teaching method to every student, and all of them can play as a result of it. I’m proud of them and they all keep in contact with me which is gratifying.
Have some of them gone on to be really full time players?

Some of them have, in other areas of the country. They do book shows, one went on to do “A Chorus Line,” and he traveled all over the country, and one of them is a studio musician in L.A., and a few of them have made livelihoods out of it, in the country/ western field. And I had a few females that went on to play metal music and were quite successful. And they keep in contact with me, particularly at Christmas time, you get all these Christmas cards, again gratifying.
